name: Reverse Kimura
description: Master Reverse Kimura in BJJ. Complete guide with safety protocols, setup from various positions, and execution. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 45%, Advanced 60%.
overview: The Reverse Kimura is a shoulder lock variation that applies the same rotational mechanics as the traditional Kimura but with a reversed grip configuration. Instead of the standard figure-four grip with your hand grabbing your own wrist behind the opponent's arm, the Reverse Kimura involves gripping your wrist in front of the opponent's arm, creating a different leverage angle and control pattern. This submission is particularly effective from standing positions, front headlocks, and scrambles where traditional Kimura grips may not be accessible. The Reverse Kimura shares the same target area and injury mechanism as the standard Kimura—the shoulder joint and rotator cuff—but the reversed grip often provides superior control in dynamic situations and allows for unique transitions to back takes and other submissions. The technique is highly valued in wrestling-based grappling and no-gi contexts where grip fighting and hand fighting create opportunities for unconventional entries. Understanding both the standard and reverse Kimura variations creates a more complete shoulder lock system that adapts to different gripping scenarios.

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 4-6 seconds minimum with constant communication
tap_signals: Verbal tap (most important for standing submissions)
Physical hand tap on any available surface
Physical tap with free hand on partner
release_protocol: Release grip completely and step back
Allow partner to externally rotate shoulder naturally
Do not force arm back to neutral position
Check with partner before continuing training
training_restrictions: Never apply quickly or explosively in training
Never continue rotation past 90 degrees in practice
Always maintain verbal communication during application
Never spike or drop weight during standing applications
Always allow partner clear tap access with free hand
Stop immediately at first sign of discomfort

key_principles: Grip reversal provides different leverage angle and control compared to standard Kimura
Wrist control must be secured before initiating shoulder rotation to prevent slippage
The reversed grip naturally drives the shoulder into internal rotation creating submission pressure
Hip positioning and body angle are critical for generating safe, progressive rotational force
The free hand controls the opponent's body or head preventing escape and maintaining position
Standing applications require exceptional balance and base to safely control descent
The submission can be applied progressively from control position or explosively in scrambles (training vs competition distinction)
setup_requirements: Secure control of opponent's wrist with your hand that will form the reverse grip
Your other arm must trap or control the opponent's elbow preventing defensive straightening
Establish superior body position—typically standing over opponent in turtle or front headlock
Create angle relative to opponent's body that allows natural rotation without forced movement
Ensure your own base is stable especially if applying from standing positions
Opponent's shoulder should be somewhat flexed or compromised making rotation mechanically easier
Clear space to finish the submission or transition if opponent defends

execution_steps.action: Establish wrist control and arm isolation
execution_steps.description: From your starting position (standing, front headlock, or scramble), secure a firm grip on your opponent's wrist with one hand. Simultaneously use your other arm to trap their elbow or upper arm. This two-point control prevents them from straightening the arm or pulling it away. Your grip should be strong but not death-gripping—you need to be able to transition to the reverse Kimura grip smoothly. Position yourself so that your opponent's arm is somewhat bent and vulnerable to rotational attack.

execution_steps.action: Thread arm through for reverse grip
execution_steps.description: Thread your controlling arm through the space between your opponent's arm and their body, positioning your hand to grab your own wrist on the opposite side of their arm. This creates the reverse figure-four configuration. The key difference from standard Kimura is that your grabbing hand reaches in front of their arm rather than behind it. This grip reversal changes the leverage angle and often provides tighter control. Ensure the grip is deep and secure before proceeding—a shallow grip will slip under pressure.

With the reverse Kimura grip secured, adjust your body position to create the optimal angle for shoulder rotation. If standing, maintain a strong base with your weight distributed properly. If from front headlock, ensure your chest pressure controls their head and prevents forward movement. Your hips should be positioned to allow you to rotate their shoulder without forcing your own body into awkward positions. The angle should feel natural—if you have to contort yourself, adjust your position before applying pressure.

Initiate the submission by slowly rotating the opponent's shoulder toward their back. The reverse grip naturally drives internal rotation when you pull your grips toward your own body. Move progressively—you should feel increasing resistance as the shoulder reaches its limit. Use your body weight and positioning rather than pure arm strength. Your free hand should maintain control of their head or body preventing them from turning into the submission to relieve pressure. Maintain constant awareness of their tap signals.

As you feel the opponent's shoulder tighten, continue the rotation slowly and progressively. In training, stop well before the finish point. In competition, you may continue to completion but always respect the tap. The reverse Kimura can finish very suddenly compared to standard Kimura due to the grip angle, so extreme caution is required. If standing, you may need to change levels or pressure them toward the ground to maintain control and finish safely. Never spike or drop your weight explosively.
execution_steps.timing: Finishing phase, 2-3 seconds with progressive increase

execution_steps.action: Transition or release based on situation
execution_steps.description: If the opponent taps, release immediately following safety protocols. If they defend successfully by turning into the lock or gripping their own gi/body, you have several options: transition to back take by following their rotation, switch to standard Kimura if the angle changes, or release and reset to maintain control without injury risk. The reverse Kimura often opens up back exposure as opponents try to relieve shoulder pressure by turning, making it an excellent setup position even if the submission itself doesn't finish.

opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: Maintain elbow control and use your body weight to prevent full extension. If they succeed in straightening, transition to other attacks like front headlock chokes or re-establish the grip from a different angle.

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Turning into the lock to relieve shoulder pressure
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: Follow their rotation and transition to back take. The reverse Kimura naturally leads to back exposure when opponents rotate to defend. Maintain your grip and use it to control their movement as you establish hooks or body lock.

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Grabbing their own gi, belt, or body to create a defensive frame
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: In no-gi this defense is less effective. In gi, you may need to break the grip by increasing rotational pressure or by using your free hand to strip their defensive grip. Alternatively, use the control to transition to other positions.

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Dropping weight or sitting to remove your standing leverage
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: Follow them to the ground maintaining your grip and superior position. The reverse Kimura transitions well from standing to ground positions. Establish side control or north-south as you bring them down, keeping the submission threat active.

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Rolling forward or granby rolling to escape
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: The reverse Kimura grip prevents most rolling escapes if maintained properly. Stay heavy on their upper body and use the grip to control their movement. If they do manage to roll, you often end up in superior position with back access or mounted position.

common_errors.error: Applying rotational pressure too quickly or explosively
common_errors.consequence: Immediate shoulder injury, torn rotator cuff, or dislocation
common_errors.correction: Always apply pressure slowly and progressively over 4-6 seconds minimum in training. Feel for increasing resistance and stop well before the breaking point. Save explosive applications only for competition if necessary.

common_errors.error: Shallow or incomplete reverse grip allowing slippage
common_errors.consequence: Loss of control, submission escapes, and wasted energy re-establishing grip
common_errors.correction: Ensure your hand reaches fully through the space and grabs your wrist with a deep, secure grip. Your forearm should be tight against their arm creating the figure-four lock. Test the grip before applying rotational pressure.

common_errors.error: Poor body positioning creating awkward angles
common_errors.consequence: Ineffective submission pressure, wasted strength, and vulnerability to counter attacks
common_errors.correction: Adjust your body angle before applying pressure. Your hips and shoulders should be positioned to allow natural rotation. If the movement feels forced or awkward, reposition before continuing.

common_errors.error: Neglecting control of opponent's head or body with free hand
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes by turning into lock, scrambling away, or countering position
common_errors.correction: Your free hand must always maintain control. From standing, control the head with your free arm. From ground positions, use body weight and positioning to prevent movement. Never focus solely on the arm lock.

common_errors.error: Continuing rotation past 90 degrees in training
common_errors.consequence: Serious injury even if partner cannot tap in time due to rapid progression
common_errors.correction: In training, stop rotation at approximately 45-60 degrees and wait for tap. The submission can complete very suddenly with the reverse grip angle, so conservative stopping points are essential for safety.

common_errors.error: Failing to maintain base when applying from standing
common_errors.consequence: Both practitioners fall uncontrollably creating injury risk beyond the submission itself
common_errors.correction: Keep feet in strong athletic stance, maintain balance throughout application, and control the descent if bringing opponent to ground. Never sacrifice your base for additional submission pressure from standing.

common_errors.error: Forcing the technique against stronger defensive grips
common_errors.consequence: Muscle strain, ineffective technique, and missed opportunity for transitions
common_errors.correction: If opponent establishes strong defensive grip, use the control to transition rather than forcing through. The reverse Kimura provides excellent positional control even if the finish isn't immediately available.

variations_and_setups.description: When controlling opponent in turtle or front headlock position, isolate the far arm and establish reverse Kimura grip. Use your head pressure and body weight to prevent forward movement while rotating the shoulder. This setup is extremely common in wrestling-based grappling.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent turtles or you establish front headlock control during scrambles

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Reverse Kimura to Back Take Transition
variations_and_setups.description: As opponent defends by turning into the lock to relieve shoulder pressure, maintain your grip and follow their rotation to take the back. The reverse Kimura naturally creates back exposure during defensive movements. Use the grip to control their rotation and establish hooks as you transition.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent successfully defends the submission by rotating toward you

variations_and_setups.description: From standing clinch with overhook control, transition to reverse Kimura grip by threading your arm through and gripping your wrist. The overhook naturally sets up the arm position for reverse grip entry. Control their posture with your free hand on their head or collar.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: During standing exchanges when you establish overhook control in clinch

variations_and_setups.description: From crucifix control on the mat, one arm is already trapped. Apply reverse Kimura grip to the trapped arm while your legs control their body. This provides extremely secure control and high finishing percentage due to their limited defensive options.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you achieve crucifix position from back control or scrambles

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the minimum application time for Reverse Kimura in training and why is this submission particularly dangerous?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Minimum 4-6 seconds with progressive pressure and constant communication. The Reverse Kimura is particularly dangerous because the reversed grip angle can cause the submission to complete more suddenly than standard Kimura, potentially injuring the opponent before they can tap. The internal rotation of the shoulder happens rapidly once the joint reaches its limit, creating high injury risk if applied too quickly. Always stop well before the finish point in training.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the grip configuration differ between standard Kimura and Reverse Kimura, and what mechanical advantage does this provide?
knowledge_assessment.answer: In standard Kimura, your grabbing hand reaches behind the opponent's arm to grip your wrist, creating a figure-four with your forearm behind their arm. In Reverse Kimura, your grabbing hand reaches in front of their arm to grip your wrist, creating the figure-four with your forearm in front of their arm. This reverse configuration often provides tighter control in dynamic situations, different leverage angles, and better control during scrambles. The reverse grip naturally drives internal rotation when you pull toward your body, making it mechanically efficient from standing and front headlock positions.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the mandatory tap signals for standing Reverse Kimura submissions and why is verbal communication especially important?
knowledge_assessment.answer: All standard tap signals apply: verbal tap, physical hand tap, foot tap, or any distress signal. Verbal tap is especially important for standing submissions because the opponent may have limited ability to physically tap while maintaining balance and defending. Additionally, standing submissions can progress to dangerous falls if not controlled, so clear communication allows both practitioners to safely manage the descent or release. Never restrict your partner's ability to verbally tap by covering their mouth or applying pressure that prevents speech.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most effective defensive response to Reverse Kimura and how should you adapt your technique when this defense occurs?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The most effective defense is turning into the lock to relieve shoulder pressure by externally rotating the shoulder. When this defense occurs, you should maintain your grip and follow their rotation to transition to back take. The reverse Kimura naturally creates back exposure as opponents rotate to defend. Rather than forcing the submission against this defense, use the superior control to establish hooks, body lock, or seat belt control for back position. This makes the reverse Kimura an excellent setup technique even when it doesn't finish directly.

knowledge_assessment.question: From what positions is the Reverse Kimura most commonly applied, and why is it particularly effective in wrestling-based grappling?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Reverse Kimura is most commonly applied from standing positions, front headlock, and scrambles. It is particularly effective in wrestling-based grappling because these contexts frequently create situations where traditional Kimura grips are not accessible but the reverse grip can be established during hand fighting. The technique also works well in no-gi grappling where grip variety is important. Wrestling exchanges often result in overhook positions, front headlock control, and scrambles where the reverse Kimura provides both submission threat and positional control.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the proper release protocol if your partner taps to Reverse Kimura from standing position?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately stop all rotational pressure, release the grip completely, and step back to create space. Allow your partner to externally rotate their shoulder naturally—never force the arm back to neutral position as this can cause additional injury. Control your partner's descent if they are off-balance to prevent falls. Check verbally with your partner before continuing training and ensure they have no shoulder discomfort. If applying from standing, be especially careful to prevent uncontrolled falls during the release by maintaining body control and stepping away safely.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must you maintain control of the opponent's head or body with your free hand during Reverse Kimura application?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Controlling the head or body with your free hand prevents the opponent from turning into the lock (the most effective defense), scrambling away, or countering your position. From standing, head control prevents forward movement and maintains your leverage. From ground positions, body pressure prevents rotation and escape attempts. Without this control, opponents can easily defend by turning toward you or creating space to pull their arm free. The reverse Kimura requires two-point control—the grip itself and body/head control—to be effective and safe.

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structures are targeted by the Reverse Kimura and what are the primary injury risks?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Reverse Kimura targets the shoulder joint and rotator cuff complex. The primary injury risks include rotator cuff tears (requiring 3-6 months recovery with potential surgery), shoulder dislocation (6-12 weeks recovery), AC joint separation (4-8 weeks), and labrum tears (6-12 months with surgery likely). The submission creates internal rotation stress on the shoulder joint, and the reversed grip angle can accelerate the breaking mechanism compared to standard Kimura. This makes controlled, progressive application absolutely critical to prevent catastrophic injury.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you recognize when the shoulder joint is approaching its rotational limit during Reverse Kimura application?
knowledge_assessment.answer: You will feel progressively increasing resistance as the shoulder approaches its limit—the movement becomes less fluid and requires more force to continue. The opponent's body will often tense, their breathing may become strained, and they may begin making sounds of discomfort. The arm will feel like it's hitting a 'wall' where further rotation requires significantly more pressure. In training, stop at the first sign of this increased resistance and wait for the tap. Never push through this barrier, as the transition from limit to injury can be instantaneous.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the proper body positioning for finishing the Reverse Kimura from standing versus from front headlock control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: From standing, maintain a strong athletic base with feet shoulder-width apart, keep your hips low for stability, and use your body weight by changing levels rather than pure arm strength to generate rotation. Control the descent if the opponent drops. From front headlock, drive chest pressure into their upper back to prevent forward movement, sprawl your hips back for base, and use the angle created by their bent-over posture to generate rotational force. In both positions, your body should be positioned to allow natural rotation without awkward angles that compromise your balance or control.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you abandon the Reverse Kimura finish and transition to positional advancement instead?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Abandon the finish when the opponent establishes a strong defensive grip you cannot break without excessive force, when they successfully straighten their arm and you cannot re-bend it, when continuing would require explosive or jerking movements, or when the angle has shifted making the submission mechanically inefficient. In all these cases, the reverse Kimura still provides excellent control for transitions—follow their defensive movements to take the back, transition to standard Kimura if they create space, or use the control to establish side control or mount. A controlled transition beats a forced submission.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the Reverse Kimura integrate into a complete shoulder lock system with other techniques?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Reverse Kimura complements the standard Kimura by covering grip scenarios where the traditional figure-four cannot be established. When opponents defend the reverse grip by straightening their arm, you can transition to standard Kimura as they bend it defensively. If they turn into the lock, the back take becomes available. If they turtle tight, the position sets up Americana-style attacks or arm triangles. The reverse Kimura also chains with guillotines from front headlock—if they defend the choke by posting, the arm becomes available for the Kimura grip. This creates a comprehensive attack system where each technique opens others.
